title: Thirty-Seven Buyers Above 300 Guilders: the Bubble Whose Popular Version Is Mostly Wrong
participants: Dutch merchant and skilled artisan buyers of tulip bulbs
Tulip trading companies and committees in Dutch towns

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: There was a trade and there were high prices, and the dossier keeps both: "the most expensive tulips of all cost around 5,000 guilders (the price of a well-appointed house)". What there was not was breadth — the historian "was able to identify only 37 people who spent more than 300 guilders on bulbs, around the yearly wage of a master craftsman. Many tulips were far cheaper."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structure was a forward market in goods that physically did not exist yet: "None of the bulbs were actually available – they were all planted in the ground – and no money would be exchanged until the bulbs could be handed over in May or June." Paper changed hands; nothing else could.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog in this dossier is retrospective, and it is the reason the node is worth carrying. The story that circulates — irrational frenzy, chimney-sweeps and aristocrats alike, bulbs traded ten times a day, bankrupts in the canals, a ruined economy — is repeated "whether by casual tweeters or in widely read economics textbooks by luminaries such as John Kenneth Galbraith". The archives say otherwise.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall to speak of, and no ruin either. Because settlement was months away, "those who lost money in the February crash did so only notionally: they might not get paid later. Anyone who had both bought and sold a tulip on paper since the summer of 1636 had lost nothing. Only those waiting for payment were in trouble, and they were people able to bear the loss."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There was no official containment because there was no official intervention: the "government" of the federal Dutch Republic "did not shut down the trade, and indeed reacted slowly and hesitantly to demands from some traders and city councils to resolve disputes. The provincial court of Holland suggested that people talk it out among themselves and try to stay out of the courts: no government regulation here."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A wealthy trading republic with a taste for collectable rarities, and a seasonal product whose prized striped and speckled forms were hard to cultivate and therefore genuinely scarce.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The story itself — the standing comparison that every later episode is measured against, from the South Sea Bubble to railways to dotcom stocks to Bitcoin, which the article opens by listing.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The legend is self-renewing: each new boom is explained by reference to tulip mania, and each retelling reinforces a version of tulip mania that the archives do not support, which is then available to explain the next boom.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That tulip mania was mass irrationality — everyone from chimney-sweeps to aristocrats trading the same bulb ten times a day at the price of houses, ruined bankrupts drowning themselves in canals, and the Dutch economy wrecked until the government stepped in.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Every element of that is contradicted by the archival work this article reports. Participation was narrow: only 37 people identified as spending more than 300 guilders, mostly wealthy merchants, with buyers and sellers "connected to each other by family, religion, or neighbourhood". Turnover was modest: "I never found a chain of buyers longer than five, and most were far shorter". The trading was "relatively calm, located in taverns and neighbourhoods rather than on the stock exchange", and increasingly organised through companies and expert committees. The plague explanation fails on timing, the biggest rises coming in January 1637 as plague waned. Losses were largely notional because settlement had not arrived, and "No one drowned themselves in canals. I found not a single bankrupt in these years who could be identified as someone dealt the fatal financial blow by tulip mania." The economy "was left completely unaffected", and the state did not shut the trade down. The one thing that survives is that the most expensive bulbs really did cost about 5,000 guilders.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A luxury market in a rapidly enriching trading republic, in bulbs that were genuinely scarce and hard to cultivate in their prized forms. Peak prices around 5,000 guilders for the most expensive bulbs, against only 37 identified buyers spending more than 300 guilders — roughly a master craftsman’s annual wage. Trading conducted in taverns and neighbourhoods, increasingly organised through town companies and committees of experts, with sellers mainly selling to people they knew and no observed chain of buyers longer than five. A crash in February 1637 attributed to fears of oversupply and unsustainable rises in the first five weeks of the year, not to naive entrants. Losses largely notional because no bulbs or money had yet changed hands. No identified bankruptcy caused by it, no effect on the Dutch economy, and no government suppression of the trade — the provincial court of Holland told the parties to settle it among themselves.

citations.title: Anne Goldgar, "Tulip mania: the classic story of a Dutch financial bubble is mostly wrong", The Conversation, 12 February 2018
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full. SOURCE CHARACTER: a signed article by a historian summarising her own archival research (the author states "My years of research in Dutch archives while working on a book, Tulipmania: Money, Honor and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age"). It is journalism reporting scholarship, not a primary record, and is tiered and attributed as such. It is cited here because it is an unusually direct statement of the gap between the popular story and the archives. The author sets out the received version — that tulip mania "was irrational", "was a frenzy", that "Everyone in the Netherlands was involved, from chimney-sweeps to aristocrats", that bulbs were "traded sometimes 10 times a day", that "Tulips were sold for crazy prices – the price of houses", that "Desperate bankrupts threw themselves in canals", and that "the economy of Holland was ruined" — and answers: "The trouble is, most of it is untrue." THE CORRECTIONS, each with its archival basis: on rationality, tulips were "a newish luxury product in a country rapidly expanding its wealth and trade networks", and "it wasn’t irrational to pay a high price for something that was generally considered valuable, and for which the next person might pay even more". On frenzy: "for much of the period trading was relatively calm, located in taverns and neighbourhoods rather than on the stock exchange", becoming "increasingly organised, with companies set up in various towns to grow, buy, and sell, and committees of experts emerged to oversee the trade"; and "Far from bulbs being traded hundreds of times, I never found a chain of buyers longer than five, and most were far shorter." On the plague explanation: "this seems not to have existed. Despite an epidemic going on during 1636, the biggest price rises occurred in January 1637, when plague (mainly a summer disease) was on the wane." On prices and participation: "Although it’s true that the most expensive tulips of all cost around 5,000 guilders (the price of a well-appointed house), I was able to identify only 37 people who spent more than 300 guilders on bulbs, around the yearly wage of a master craftsman. Many tulips were far cheaper", and those top buyers "came from the wealthy merchant class and were well able to afford the bulbs"; participants were "relatively small" in number, "mainly from the merchant and skilled artisan class", with many "connected to each other by family, religion, or neighbourhood. Sellers mainly sold to people they knew." On the crash: it came "not because of naive and uninformed people entering the market, but probably through fears of oversupply and the unsustainability of the great price rise in the first five weeks of 1637", and because the bulbs were in the ground with no money due until May or June, "those who lost money in the February crash did so only notionally: they might not get paid later. Anyone who had both bought and sold a tulip on paper since the summer of 1636 had lost nothing." On the human and economic damage: "No one drowned themselves in canals. I found not a single bankrupt in these years who could be identified as someone dealt the fatal financial blow by tulip mania", and "The Dutch economy was left completely unaffected." On the state: "The ‘government’ ... did not shut down the trade, and indeed reacted slowly and hesitantly", with the provincial court of Holland suggesting "that people talk it out among themselves and try to stay out of the courts: no government regulation here."
